records.sourceFile: Effect of Individual Environmental Heat-Stress Variables on Training and Recovery in Professional Team Sport.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Prospective field study of 45 male professional Australian Rules football players over an 8-week preseason, giving 579 outdoor training observations. Ambient temperature, relative humidity and solar radiation were recorded each session and related to GPS external load, heart rate and RPE, and to well-being and heart-rate variability over the following 48 hours, using mixed-effects models. Solar radiation was associated with less distance and less high-speed running during training, and relative humidity with higher RPE and stress; higher ambient temperature was associated with more distance and high-speed running.
records.limitations: The design is observational, from one club, in heat-acclimatized players during one Australian summer, so the associations cannot be read as causal or generalized to other squads or climates. Recovery effects were mostly null, and heart-rate variability was measured once daily, so the recovery findings are weak.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read the paper as showing that solar radiation and humidity cause a fixed loss of work capacity, when the effects are model-based associations within one club's training sessions.

changes: findings: temperature effect on distance reported as the results-text value only (19.2 m/min; 95% CI, 18.0 to 21.4 m/min; P < .001) instead of giving both values; abstract 19.7 conflict kept in limitations
findings: added humidity body mass loss (-215 g) and temperature-linked rises in mean HR (4.8 bpm) and RPE (0.3 AU) so the 'more work with higher temperature' result is not read in isolation
limitations: added convenience sample and single subtropical site; clarified which value is reported

records.sourceFile: Effect of velocity loss during squat training on neuromuscular performance.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Randomized trial in 33 young men (physically active sports science students with 1 to 3 years of resistance training, injury-free) who completed 8 weeks of squat training at the same relative loads, with sets stopped at 10%, 30% or 45% velocity loss (n = 11 per group after one dropout per group). All groups improved squat strength and muscle endurance; the only significant group by time interaction was for countermovement jump, where the 10% group (11.9%) gained more than the 45% group, and sprint changes favored the 10% group descriptively (-2.4% vs -1.8% and -0.5%) without a significant interaction. No EMG change was significant in any group.
records.limitations: Participants were physically active students rather than competitive athletes, all were men, and there was no non-training control group. Strength was estimated from a load-velocity equation rather than measured directly, and the Abstract and Discussion describe jump and sprint advantages for the 10% group more broadly than the between-group statistics support.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read the 10% velocity-loss result as an optimal set-stopping rule for all athletes, when the study used one exercise, young recreational men and an 8-week period.

changes: populations: removed Male Athletes and Healthy Athletes because participants were 'physically active sports science students', not athletes; kept Adult / Recreational

findings/evidenceSummary/tldr: sprint advantage for 10% stated as if established -> no significant interaction for sprint ('A significant "time x group" interaction (p < 0.05) was only found for CMJ'); VL45% did not improve sprint ('except in sprint performance')
limitations: added the Abstract sprint claim to the Abstract-versus-Results conflict
practicalImplications/athleteDev: removed claims of larger sprint gains
verification.residualConcerns: Sample is physically active students rather than athletes.

records.sourceFile: Effectiveness of Accentuated Eccentric Loading - Contingent on Concentric Load.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Crossover laboratory study of 21 resistance-trained men (age 24.0 [4.2] y) who completed back-squat sets with accentuated eccentric loading (AEL, 120% 1-RM eccentric via weight releasers) or traditional loading at 65% and 80% 1-RM. At 65%, AEL was followed by faster eccentric velocity and greater eccentric power, and faster concentric velocity and higher mean power in repetitions 3 and 4; at 80%, eccentric power was greater but concentric velocity and power did not improve. The authors report higher concentric peak force after AEL at both loads (187.8 N at 65%; 133.8 N at 80%).
records.limitations: This is a single-session acute study with no training outcome, follow-up, or sport task, so it cannot show chronic adaptation. It tests one exercise (back squat) with weight releasers at two concentric loads in healthy men.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read the 65% concentric gain as a general AEL benefit for squat training, when the same protocol gave no concentric velocity or power gain at 80% 1-RM and the effect was measured within one session.

changes: populations: Male Athletes, Healthy Athletes, Mixed / Unspecified -> Adult / Recreational (sample is 'Resistance-trained men (N = 21)', not athletes)

paper.practicalImplications: 'first repetition after weight release may be slower with AEL' generalised a finding seen only at 80% -> limited to 80% concentric mean velocity ('concentric mean velocity of repetition 1 was lower after AEL80 compared with TRA80')
verification.residualConcerns: Table 1 shows a significant protocol-by-repetition interaction for concentric mean power at 80% (F2,40 = 14.53, P < .01) while the Discussion says no concentric power increase occurred at 80%; the record follows the Discussion and flags this in limitations. Abstract gives P = .01 and Results P < .01 for concentric peak force at 65%.

records.sourceFile: Effects of Resistance and Speed on Electromyographic Activity of Thigh and Gluteal Muscles in Elite Athletes throughout Resisted Sprint Running.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Within-session comparison of 37 injury-free elite athletes (27 women, 10 men; track and field, rugby sevens and bobsleigh) who sprinted 40 m unresisted and against robotic horizontal resistance equal to 25% and 75% of body mass (sled-equivalent). Surface EMG from eight thigh and gluteal muscles, modelled against normalised speed, showed hamstring stance-phase activity rising with speed (+17.9% unresisted) and falling with resistance, with quadriceps showing the opposite pattern. Biceps femoris long head showed the largest speed-related increase and semitendinosus the largest resistance-related decrease among the hamstrings.
records.limitations: Acute, single-session EMG study with surface electrodes, two resistance levels, a fixed condition order (unresisted, then 25%, then 75%), and conditions compared at normalised rather than absolute speed. Sprint distance differed by condition (40, 25 and 20 m), 12 of 49 recruited athletes were excluded, and the sample mixed sex and sports, so the results describe activation patterns, not training adaptation or neural drive.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read these EMG patterns as proof that resisted sprints selectively train the quadriceps or specific hamstring heads, or as a basis for return-to-sport progression, when the study is a single session in injury-free athletes and measures no training or injury outcome.

changes: paper.citation: 'et al.' after 5 authors -> 6 authors listed (adds Hollville E) per house rule

paper.tldr: 'In elite sprinters' -> sample is track and field, rugby sevens and bobsleigh athletes ('elite track and field (10 females and 5 males), rugby seven (14 females and 5 males) and bobsleigh (3 females)')
paper.athleteDev: 'the resistance chosen should match the acceleration phase being trained' was untested prescriptive advice -> states this was not tested

paper.findings: added Table 2 range and that the 60% to 66% proportions were not significant ('Only the ST and SM muscles presented no significant change in the R75 condition'); late-swing BFlh claim scoped to the unresisted sprint-phase comparison
screeningLimitations: added fixed condition order (authors note no crossover design) and 49 recruited, 37 analysed
sports: Mixed / General Sport -> Track & Field, Rugby, Other Sport (bobsleigh)
verification.residualConcerns: Results text says BFlh stance proportion went 'from 97% in R0 to 74% in R75' but Table 2 shows BFlh R0 = 100 (97 is BFsh). Discussion claims 'consistent increases ... for 90% of the participants', which overstates Table 2. The authors' practical suggestions (earlier resisted sprinting after hamstring injury; GMed-focused exercises) are untested and are flagged as such in the record.

records.sourceFile: Effects of forearm wearable resistance during accelerated sprints - From a standing start position.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Acute within-athlete comparison in 14 healthy male track and field athletes (age 20.6 years, 100 m best 11.40 s) doing 30 m sprints from a standing two-point start, unloaded versus with 2 percent body mass forearm wearable resistance. The authors report no significant change in 10 m or 30 m sprint time, a significant drop in step frequency in acceleration phases 2 and 3, and no significant kinetic differences.
records.limitations: This is a single-session study with 14 athletes and no training intervention, so it cannot show training adaptations or long-term overload benefit. The abstract's step velocity result is not supported by the step velocity values in Table 2.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read the lower step frequency as proof that forearm loading overloads sprint mechanics, but this was an acute effect and the paper does not test whether training with these loads improves sprint performance.

changes: populations: added Adult / Recreational alongside Collegiate; participants described as 'recreational track and field male athletes' and as 'healthy collegiate male individuals'
paper.methods: specified one unloaded and two loaded trials with the fastest loaded trial analysed ('The one UL trial, and the fastest FWR trials were used')
paper.findings: replaced draft percentages with Table 2 values; clarified contact/flight time and step length changes were non-significant
paper.limitations: added that starred step frequency effect size CIs include zero and contact time CIs exclude zero, further table/text conflicts
paper.practicalImplications: 'did not noticeably slow' -> 'did not significantly slow' (mean times were 0.04 s slower)
verification.residualConcerns: Statistical reporting is internally inconsistent (abstract step velocity claim vs Table 2; CIs vs significance flags). Competition level is described as both recreational and collegiate.

records.sourceFile: Effects of horizontally vs vertically loaded resistance exercises on performance and muscle architecture.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Six-week randomized training study in 19 resistance-trained adults (15 men, 4 women), with 10 in a horizontally loaded program (hip thrust, reverse hyperextension, horizontal jumps) and 9 in a vertically loaded program (squat, step-up, vertical jumps), both with equal total repetitions. Group by time interactions favored horizontal training for 1RM hip thrust (Table III means +21.0 versus +1.8 percent) and standing long jump (+7.0 versus +1.0 percent), and vertical training for 1RM squat (+9.0 versus -0.3 percent) and vastus medialis thickness (+4.0 versus -9.0 percent), with no interaction for countermovement jump or 20 m sprint.
records.limitations: The groups were small (9 and 10 analyzed, below the 11 per group planned) and the program lasted only six weeks. Many reported statistics are internally inconsistent or implausible (text versus table percentages, an effect size of 0.998, p-values that do not match their F or r values, and muscle thickness reported in mm at values near 1.5 to 4), so exact magnitudes should not be relied on.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read the program differences as established transfer to sport performance, but sprint and vertical jump outcomes did not differ between programs, participants were not athletes, and the statistical reporting has multiple errors.

changes: populations: removed Male Athletes and Female Athletes -> Adult / Recreational; sample was 'Nineteen resistance-trained individuals', not athletes

evidenceSummary/findings: replaced text-only percentages with Table III/IV means per abstract-vs-table rule (hip thrust +21.0 vs +1.8%, squat +9.0 vs -0.3%, SLJ +7.0 vs +1.0%, VM thickness +4.0 vs -9.0%) and noted the text values
paper.abstract: 'Vertical jump improved similarly in both groups' -> only a time main effect (P = 0.047), changes below the stated 5.4 cm minimal difference

paper.limitations/screeningLimitations: added implausible statistics (eta2 0.998; F = 10.946 with P = 0.050; r = -0.487 with P = 0.004 in n = 19; muscle thickness in 'mm' at 1.4-4.2), abstract vs Methods group characteristics conflict
paper.practicalImplications/athleteDev: removed claim that both programs improved vertical jump similarly as a positive finding
verification.residualConcerns: Statistical reporting in this paper has multiple errors; magnitudes are uncertain. Muscle thickness units appear to be cm mislabeled as mm.

records.sourceFile: Effects of resistance exercise combined with vascular     occlusion on muscle function in athletes..pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Three-group experimental study of 17 young male elite rugby players over 8 weeks (twice weekly): low-intensity knee extension at about 50% 1RM with vascular occlusion (LIO, n = 6), the same load without occlusion (LI, n = 6), and a control group that did not train (n = 5). The LIO group improved isometric and isokinetic knee extension strength (isokinetic gain 14.3% vs 3.2% in LI, averaged across velocities), quadriceps cross-sectional area (+12.3%, p = 0.002) and fatigue resistance, while the LI group showed no significant strength change.
records.limitations: Only 5 to 6 players per group, with no randomization described, MRI measured in the occlusion group only, and no tendon or injury outcome. Results come from one 8-week block in highly trained players and may not transfer to other athletes or to injury settings.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read this as proof that occlusion training is a better strength method than heavy loading, but the study compared occlusion with a light-load control only and did not test heavy training.

changes: practicalImplications/athleteDev: implied a between-group size comparison -> size was measured in the occlusion group only ('Measurements were made only for the LIO group'); strength and endurance comparisons kept
year: checked, 2002 is correct (journal header 'Eur J Appl Physiol (2002) 86: 308-314'; accepted 2001, online 16 January 2002)

records.sourceFile: Electromyographic Comparison of Flywheel Inertial Leg Curl and Nordic Hamstring Exercise Among Soccer Players.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Within-subject crossover laboratory study of 15 male amateur soccer players (age 22.9 years) who performed five repetitions each of the Nordic hamstring exercise and the flywheel inertial leg curl. The authors report similar biceps femoris and semitendinosus activation in the lower eccentric phase and higher flywheel activation in the lower concentric phase (for example, 20% to 35% higher in the semitendinosus).

records.sourceFile: Enhancement of Mood but not Performance in Elite Athletes With Transcranial Direct-Current Stimulation.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Crossover, counterbalanced, sham-controlled, double-blind laboratory study of 8 healthy male elite triathletes. Each athlete received 20 minutes of active anodal tDCS over the motor cortex (C3, 2 mA) or sham on separate days, then an 800-m freestyle swim test. Vigor on the Brunel Mood Scale was higher with active tDCS after stimulation (P = .018) and after swimming (P = .022), but 800-m time did not differ (596 s active vs 599 s sham; P = .346).
records.limitations: Only 8 men were tested before the competition season, with a single stimulation protocol and a cephalic electrode montage, so the result cannot be generalized to women, other sports or other tDCS settings. No measures of cortical excitability or brain activity were taken, and the condition order was counterbalanced but randomization is not described.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read the vigor result as a performance benefit, but the swim time did not improve and the mood effect comes from a small sample.

changes: limitations/screeningLimitations: said performance was judged by magnitude-based inference rather than a significance test -> paired t test (P = .346) plus MBI ('paired Student t tests'); added that order was counterbalanced with no randomization described
findings: added that other BRUMS domains had no condition effect and adverse-effect results ('Tingling 8 / 8')

records.sourceFile: Enhancing athletic performance with complex contrast training - A Delphi study of elite strength and conditioning coaches.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Three-round Delphi survey of elite strength and conditioning coaches (38 in round one, 36 men and 2 women; 37 and 34 in later rounds) on how they prescribe complex contrast training for team sport athletes. Of 139 statements, 31 reached the 80% agreement threshold (27 in round two, 4 in round three), including four sets per pairing, 3 to 4 repetitions at 85-90% 1RM with two repetitions in reserve for the strength exercise, and bodyweight to 30% 1RM for the power exercise.
records.limitations: The evidence is coach opinion from 34 to 38 respondents, mostly in Australia and New Zealand, with no athlete outcome data, so it describes practice rather than effectiveness. Athlete characteristics are not reported.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read a coach consensus on typical settings as proof that complex contrast training improves performance or saves time; the study measured opinion, not outcomes.

records.sourceFile: Enhancing team sports performance - A case study of the optimal post-warm-up time window.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Single-day repeated-measures study with no control group in 19 college athletes (basketball, football, handball, swimming or fitness). Countermovement jump, 20-m sprint, handgrip and saliva markers were measured before a team-sport warm-up and at 5 and 10 minutes after it. Jump height rose from 0.35 to 0.38 m at 5 minutes and stayed at 0.37 m at 10 minutes, and 20-m sprint time improved from 3.83 s to 3.60 s at 5 minutes, then 3.68 s at 10 minutes.

records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read the 5-10 minute window as a proven timing rule for kickoff, or the 5 to 10 minute sprint slowing as a real decline, but there was no control group and the 5 vs 10 minute sprint difference was not significant.

records.sourceFile: Evaluating a 14-week neck strengthening protocol for neuromuscular indicators associated with head and neck trauma.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: A single-group, pre-post pilot in 18 healthy college-aged adults (9 men, 9 women, 18 to 29 years; 20 consented, 2 withdrew) who trained for 14 weeks with a helmet-mounted neck-strengthening device, with no control group. records.evidenceSummary: Review article by four sport and exercise scientists giving evidence-based recommendations for blood flow restriction (BFR) training. It summarizes studies of BFR with low-load resistance exercise (about 20 to 40% 1RM), BFR at rest, and BFR with walking or cycling, in mostly small samples of untrained, older, rehabilitation and athletic participants. It reports that BFR with low-load resistance exercise enhances hypertrophy and strength, and that BFR alone can attenuate disuse atrophy during immobilization.
records.limitations: No search method is described, so the selection of studies cannot be checked. Several pressure and cuff recommendations rest on unpublished laboratory data or on small studies, and the authors state that the circumference-based pressure guidance has not been tested for training adaptation.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read BFR with low-load training as a substitute for heavy strength training for athletes, when the review reports smaller 1RM gains with BFR alone (8.7%) than with high-load (19.9%) or combined training (15.3%) in one study and recommends adding BFR to high-load training rather than replacing it.

changes: populations: Healthy Athletes and Adult / Recreational -> removed; this is a review spanning clinical, elderly, untrained and athletic cohorts, not an athlete sample
